episodes.title: Episode 03: Three hundred rounds of nothing, and what was wrong
notes: r2 flat at 69-70% (goal checks, 1,000 games) from iteration ~100 to 357
Net 357 alone 66.7%; search 100 / 400 / 1,600 simulations 67.3% / 70.2% / 69.5%; the net predicts the searched buy 98% of the time
Value head error on fresh games 0.68 → 0.92 → 1.17 (warm, iteration 100, 357) while the training log showed 0.19; always predicting a draw: 0.97
Fix (offline study, 3,000 games): a new value head trained on the search's root value: held-out error 1.24 → 0.70; run r3 trains this way
transcript: At the end of the last episode, the player had passed its goal. After a hundred rounds of self-play, it won about sixty nine percent of the fresh games against the evolved priority list. Then I let it run for another day. It played two hundred and fifty more rounds, a quarter of a million games. And the number did not move. Sixty nine, seventy, sixty eight, sixty nine. This episode is about why.

The first clue came from asking a simple question. How much does the search actually add? I took the newest network and played the same thousand fresh games four ways. The network alone, with no search at all, won sixty seven percent. With a hundred imagined games per buy, sixty seven. With four hundred, seventy. With sixteen hundred, seventy again. At the very start of training, the search had added seven points on top of the network. Now it added three, and four times more thinking added nothing.

The training log showed the same thing from the other side. The network now predicted the search's chosen card ninety eight percent of the time. That is the trap in this kind of learning. The search teaches the network, and the network guides the search. When they agree on almost everything, self-play has nothing left to teach.

My first idea was that the search was too timid. The network was very sure of itself. For most buys it put ninety nine percent on a single card. A search guided by such a confident network barely looks at anything else. So I made the network's advice softer inside the search, in two ways. A mild softening did nothing. Sixty nine percent. A strong one, where a quarter of the advice was spread evenly over every card, was a disaster. The player dropped to forty eight percent, worse than the opponent it started from.

That disaster was the real clue. When a search looks at every card, and its judgement of each position is noisy, some bad card will look good just by luck. The search then picks exactly that card. It is the same trap as picking the best of many noisy tests. So the problem was not how widely the search looked. It was how well it judged what it saw.

Remember that the search judges a new position half by the network's own win estimate, and half by playing the game out. So I tested the network's win estimate on six hundred fresh games. The result surprised me. It was worse than useless. A guess of fifty fifty for every position would have been more accurate. And it had got worse during training. At the start its error was point six eight, after a hundred rounds point nine two, and at the end one point one seven.

Yet the training log said the error had fallen to point two. The log measured it on the training games themselves. Each game gives about thirty five positions, and they all share one final result. The network saw each of them about ten times. So it learned to recognise the games, not to judge the positions. It memorised.

The fix came from an offline study. I recorded three thousand fresh games, trained different versions on four fifths of them, and tested on the rest. Less training, lower weights, stronger penalties, none of it helped much. Two things did. First, throw away the old win estimate and train a new one on top of the same network. Second, don't teach it the final result of the game. Teach it the search's own estimate for that position. A game's result is one coin flip shared by thirty five positions. The search's estimate is a separate, careful measurement for each one. Together, the error dropped from one point two four to point seven.

Did the player get stronger with the better estimate? Only a little, so far. Seventy percent with the mixed judgement, about the same as before. Seventy with the network's estimate alone, up from sixty eight. So now a new run is training with these fixes, to see whether an honest judge lets self-play climb again. I'll tell you how it goes.

episodes.title: Episode 02: Two failures that shaped the method
notes: Leaf value from the net alone: 51% → 53% → 48% vs the GA at 100 → 400 → 1,600 simulations; half net, half GA rollout: 52% → 58% → 60% (600 games each)
Run r1 trained on visit shares: the net alone fell from 51.7% to 24.3% in one iteration
Run r2 (expert iteration: learn the chosen buy, no root noise): goal checks 63.5% at iteration 10, 65.2% at 20, ~69% from 100
From iteration 7, 20% of self-play games against Big Money / Smithy-BM / Witch-BM to stop the drift against simple bots
transcript: In the last episode I described the plan. A network guides a search, the search teaches the network, round after round. This episode is about the two things that went wrong first, because they explain why the player works the way it does now.

The first failure was about how to score a position. When the search reaches a new position, it needs a number: how good is this for me? The textbook answer is to ask the network. So I tested that first, against the evolved priority list, on six hundred games each.

With the network's guess alone, a hundred imagined games per buy scored about fifty one percent. Four hundred scored fifty three. And sixteen hundred scored forty eight. More thinking made the player worse. The reason is that the network is bad at guessing the winner. After imitation it could copy the evolved list's buys ninety eight percent of the time. But its guess of who would win was barely better than a coin. Dominion between two similar players stays close until late. A search that trusts a bad judge just finds the positions where the judge is most wrong, and the more it searches, the better it finds them.

The fix was to mix. Half the score comes from the network, half from actually playing the game out with the evolved list. A single playout is noisy, but it is honest, and the noise averages out over four hundred of them. With the mix, the scores were fifty two, fifty eight and sixty percent. Now more thinking helps, as it should.

The second failure was about what the network learns. AlphaZero teaches the network the share of attention the search gave each move. If the search tried Gold two hundred times and Silver a hundred, the network learns two thirds Gold, one third Silver. I started the first real run that way. One round later, the network on its own had fallen from fifty two percent to twenty four percent against the evolved list. It had collapsed.

Here is why. In Dominion, many buys are almost equally good. When the options are that close, the search spreads its attention mostly by what the network already believed, plus some random noise added on purpose to make it explore. So the attention shares were mostly the network's own opinion with noise on top. Training on that taught the network to be vague and noisy. The search still held up, because the playouts carried it. But the network itself was learning nothing true.

I tried one more idea from a newer paper, a target that reweights the network's opinion by what the search found. With a network as confident as this one, it barely moved away from the network's opinion at all.

What worked is called expert iteration. The network learns only the one card the search finally chose. No shares, and no added noise at the top of the search. Exploration comes from two other places instead. In the first six turns, the player picks its buy at random in proportion to the search's attention. And three games in ten are played against the evolved list rather than against itself.

That second run started from the same imitation network. After ten rounds, the fresh check said sixty three and a half percent. After twenty rounds, sixty five, which was the goal. After a hundred, about sixty nine.

One more adjustment came early. In the first five rounds, the score against the evolved list rose, but the score against three simple bots, like one that buys only money and Provinces, slowly fell. The player was learning to beat one opponent at the cost of general strength. So from round seven, two games in ten are played against those simple bots. Against them it stayed near seventy eight percent from then on.
So by the end of the first day, the goal was passed. In the next episode I'll tell you what happened over the following three hundred rounds, which is mostly that nothing happened, and why.

episodes.title: Episode 01: How a card game player learns to buy by imagining shuffles
notes: Dominion's buy decision: treasure, victory cards or one of 10 action cards dealt per game
The opponent and the warm start: dominion-v1's evolved priority lists (GA genomes), which also play every non-buy decision on both sides
The net: 175 inputs, two hidden layers of 128, a buy distribution and a win estimate
The search: 400 simulations per buy, every hidden card reshuffled in each (IS-MCTS with determinization); leaf = half net, half GA rollout
The goal: 65% of 1,000 fresh games against the GA base genome
transcript: Welcome to the first episode about this project. It teaches a computer player to make one kind of decision in the card game Dominion: what to buy. I want this episode to explain how it works, so that the later ones make sense.

First, the game. In Dominion every player starts with a small deck of ten cards. Each turn you draw five, play them, count your coins, and buy one new card. Treasure makes later turns richer. Victory cards score points, but they clog your hand. And ten action cards are dealt for each game, so every game has a different set of options. The game ends when the Provinces run out. Most points wins.

The buy is the hard part. Say you have six coins on turn nine. A Gold makes every later turn richer. A Duchy is three points now and a dead card forever after. A Witch hands your opponent a curse every time you play it. Which one is right depends on how long the game will last, and on cards you cannot see yet.

The starting point is an older project. There, a genetic algorithm evolved priority lists. A priority list says, for example, buy a Province if you can, else a Gold, else a Witch. Those evolved lists are strong. They are also the opponent here, and they play every decision except the buy, for both players. So when this player wins more than half the games, it is because of its buys alone.

The new player has two parts. The first is a small neural network. It reads one hundred and seventy five numbers about the game: the cards each player owns, what is left in my draw pile, what is left on the table, the coins, the score. It answers two things. How likely am I to win from here? And which card would I buy?

The second part is a search. Before every buy, the player imagines the rest of the game four hundred times. In each imagined game, it reshuffles everything it cannot see. My own draw pile gets a new order. The opponent's hand and deck get dealt again from what I know they own. Then it walks down a tree of buy decisions, mine and the opponent's. The network says which buys look promising, so the search tries those first. When the walk reaches a position it has never seen, it scores it. Half of that score is the network's own guess. The other half comes from playing the game out to the end with the evolved priority list.

After four hundred imagined games, the player buys the card it tried most often. Because each imagined game used a different shuffle, the choice is good on average over the luck of the draw, instead of good for one lucky guess.

Then comes the learning loop, the idea behind AlphaZero. The player plays a thousand games, mostly against itself and some against the evolved list. Every searched buy becomes a lesson for the network: in this position, the search chose this card, and this is who won in the end. The network trains on the last five rounds of lessons. A better network guides the next search better, and the search teaches the network again.

Before any of that, the network learns by imitation. It watched twelve thousand games of the evolved lists and learned to copy their buys. So it starts as a copy of the opponent, and the search has to find where the copy can do better.

The goal was to win sixty five percent of a thousand fresh games against the evolved list, on five hundred card sets never used in training, each played from both seats. In the next episode I'll tell you how the first attempt failed within a single round, and what that taught me.
